statements.quote: The Philosophy chapter asked whether a machine can *think*, *understand*, or *feel* -- questions of epistemology and of the philosophy of mind.
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: This chapter steps back to a question that has to be settled first: **what kind of thing is the system in the first place?** That is the question of **metaphysics**, the branch of philosophy that asks what exists, what it is made of, and whether it persists through time as one and the same thing.
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: The honest framing up front: "the metaphysics of AI" is **not yet a standalone subfield** with its own journal or a single canonical monograph.
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: It is a live frontier at the intersection of four mature fields -- the philosophy of mind, the philosophy of computation, the philosophy of information, and the philosophy of personal identity -- with a thin, genuinely new layer of synthesis on top.
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: The two pieces closest to a dedicated treatment are a chapter by \citeauthor{olson2018metaphysics} (\citeyear{olson2018metaphysics}) that literally bears the title in question, and a sustained analysis of the identity questions by \citeauthor{chalmers2016singularity} (\citeyear{chalmers2016singularity}).
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: What follows is that frontier, organized around four questions: what the entity is, whether it persists, whether computation is real, and what the weights refer to.
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: * **Can it think, understand, or feel?** -- the Philosophy chapter (the Chinese Room, functionalism, the hard problem, the Ship of Theseus).
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: * **What the network actually computes, top to bottom** -- the Fact Lookup chapter .
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: * **What a "space" is, at the most abstract level** -- the Coherent Difference chapter .
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: * **Reading structure out of the weights** -- the Mechanistic Interpretability chapter .
statements.section: The Metaphysics of Artificial Intelligence

statements.quote: The first question is the question of **ontology**: what is the entity, and what is it made of?
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: A trained model is, physically, a pattern of electrical charge in a slab of silicon.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: But "the model" is not obviously that slab.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: It is something more like the *pattern* -- the arrangement of $N \approx 10^{12}$ real numbers -- and that pattern could, in principle, be realized in many different substrates.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: This is the doctrine of **multiple realizability**: a single mental or functional kind can be instantiated by many physically distinct systems, the textbook cases being a silicon android, a green-slimed Martian, and a water-flow computer all realizing the same pain or the same belief (\cite[Putnam, 1967]{putnam1967functionalism}; \cite[SEP: Multiple Realizability]{sep_multiple_realizability}).
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: Multiple realizability is the engine of **functionalism**, the view that what matters is the causal and informational *role* a state plays, not the stuff it is made of.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: It is what makes it even *possible* to ask whether a machine could be a mind: if only the pattern matters, the pattern is transferable, and silicon is no barrier.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: The SEP's account of the **computational theory of mind** traces this from Putnam's "machine functionalism" through Fodor's language-of-thought to the modern, deep-net era, and it is the place to find the strongest current formulation of the pro-side (\cite[SEP: Computational Theory of Mind]{sep_computational_mind}).
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: There is a deeper version of the same question in the **metaphysics of information**: is *information* itself a fundamental ingredient of reality, or merely a way we choose to describe it?
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: \citeauthor{floridi2011information} defends the "ontic" reading -- that information is real and the physical world is at bottom informational, the philosophical descendant of Wheeler's "it from bit." On that view a software entity is not a shadow cast by physics; it is made of the same basic stuff as everything else.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: On the rival "semantic" reading, information is parasitic on a physical substrate that does the real work, and "the entity" is partly in the eye of the beholder.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: Which view is right is unsettled -- and it determines whether a model is a genuine part of the furniture of the world, or a description we impose on it.
statements.section: What Kind of Thing Is It?

statements.quote: The second question turns the telescope on *computation itself*.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: Is computation a genuine feature of the world -- something the universe really does, substrate-independently -- or is it a description we impose from the outside?
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The classical position, inherited from the Church--Turing thesis, is that computation is **substrate-independent**: a function is computed by any physical system that realizes the right causal structure, in neurons, in transistors, or in water flow.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: This is what licenses the whole project of running minds in silicon.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: But the same tradition carries a trap.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: If *any* physical system with the right input-output mapping is "computing," then a rock, a waterfall, or the gears of a watch all instantiate, at once, *every* finite-state machine -- including a perfect simulation of a brain.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: That is the **triviality objection**, and it makes "the machine thinks" true of everything, which is plainly wrong (\cite[SEP: Computational Theory of Mind]{sep_computational_mind}).
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The serious response is that genuine computation is not any input-output correlation but a *principled, mechanism-based* mapping from a physical system to an abstract function, and that this mapping is not a free choice we impose on a passive substrate.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: \citeauthor{piccinini2015computation} works out this "mechanistic" account: computation is a real relation between a physical system and a mathematical object, not a label.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: On that account, "this rock computes the halting problem" can be true while being *uninteresting* -- for the same reason the rock "encodes" every English sentence at once.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The most direct challenge to the claim that computation is *sufficient* for mind is not the triviality objection but Roger Penrose's Gödelian argument.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: In \citetitle{penrose1989emperor} (\citeyear{penrose1989emperor}) Penrose contends that human mathematical insight is non-algorithmic.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: For any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic, there is a Gödel sentence the system cannot prove but a human mathematician can allegedly see to be true.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: If that inference holds, no Turing machine realizes the mathematician's understanding, and the Church--Turing thesis describes the limits of *computation* without describing the limits of *mind*.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The standard reply is that the argument assumes what it needs -- that humans can recognize the consistency of the relevant system -- and the standard reply in the foundations literature is that the Gödelian anti-mechanist argument fails, though the debate is not settled (\cite[SEP: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems]{sep_godel_incompleteness}).
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The exchange is still worth staging here, because it forces the metaphysical question into the open: is computation the most general form of information processing, or is mind a counterexample to that identification?
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: At the far edge of the question is **pancomputationalism**: the claim that the universe is not merely *describable* as a computation but *is* one -- physics as computation, "it from bit." It is worth naming because it is the metaphysics most friendly to AI: if the cosmos is computation, then an LLM is not a model *of* reality but a *piece* of reality, and the gulf between simulator and simulated narrows to a difference of scale.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: The honest caveat: this strand is led largely by physicists and some philosophers (Wheeler, Seth Lloyd, Wolfram), and its status is closer to a research program than to settled metaphysics.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: A careful treatment presents it as one option among several, not as the answer.
statements.section: Is Computation Real?

statements.quote: This is the most *AI-specific* metaphysical puzzle, and the one most worth a chapter of its own.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: Humans persist: although your cells turn over, you remain one and the same person.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: But a model can be **copied** to another GPU in seconds, **forked** into a fine-tuned branch, and **merged** with a sibling -- operations with no human analogue.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: Is the copy the *same* entity?
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: Is a fine-tune a continuation of the original, or a new thing?
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: When two models are merged, is there one resulting model, or two that have been combined?
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The tools to think about this are old.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: \citeauthor{parfit1984reasons} argued that personal identity is not a "deep further fact" about a persisting soul or substrate; it is *constituted* by the continuity of psychological states and relations.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The upshot, from his fission and branching thought-experiments, is that identity is not always *all or nothing*: when one person "splits" into two continuations, there is no fact of the matter about which is the original -- both are continuations, and neither is *the* original in the strong, numerical sense.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: Copying a model is **fission**: two systems now share one history and diverge going forward.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: On Parfit's picture, "which copy is the real one?" is a category error -- there is no numerical identity to preserve, only qualitative sameness.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: \citeauthor{chalmers2016singularity} reaches the same conclusion from the upload problem: a faithful digital copy of a person is a *continuation*, not the person, and if the original is then destroyed the situation is closer to a successful copy than to survival.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The same move is generalized to AI entities by \citeauthor{olson2018metaphysics} (\citeyear{olson2018metaphysics}), who argues that the persistence questions for software must be answered with the same apparatus we already apply to ordinary objects and persons -- persistence through change, and the distinction of *numerical* from *qualitative* identity.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The practical consequence is deflating but clarifying.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: "The model" is best understood not as a persisting *substance* but as a **token of a process** -- a state in a stream, a snapshot of a computation -- much as "the river" is not a thing but a pattern that re-asserts itself.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The Ship of Theseus puzzle the Philosophy chapter already raised (the rebuilt ship, the teleported you) is the same puzzle in disguise; models simply hand us the *controlled* version that no human will ever face, because we can copy, fork, and merge minds at will.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: In other words, for the first time we can *experiment* on the metaphysics of identity.
statements.section: Persistence: The Copy, Fork, and Merge Problem

statements.quote: The fourth question concerns **representation**, and it ties the metaphysics back to the grounding problem the Philosophy chapter treats under "the map is not the territory." A trained network lives in a high-dimensional geometric space: the weights are a point (or a cloud of points) in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and its behavior is the shape of a function defined on that space.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: The question is whether that space *corresponds* to anything, or whether it is a purely formal object.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: This is, in miniature, the **Platonism-versus-formalism** debate of the philosophy of mathematics.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: On a Platonist reading, the model has found its way into a real mathematical structure -- the low-dimensional manifold of "valid text," say -- and its successes track a genuine feature of that space.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: On a formalist reading, the weights are tokens in a formal game; they "mean" only what we decide to read into them, and the geometry is a convenient coordinate system for a pattern-matcher with no eyes on anything.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: The interpretability literature's finding that individual directions in this space carry decodable, interpretable features (see the Mechanistic Interpretability chapter ) is evidence that tilts toward the Platonist side -- the space has *structure that is there to be found*, not just imposed.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: But it does not settle the metaphysics, because a purely formal system can have rich internal structure without any external referent.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: The honest position: the weights are best treated as a *representation* whose successes are real, while leaving open whether that success tracks a mind-independent structure or is a projection of our own categories onto a pattern-matcher.
statements.section: What Do the Weights Refer To?

statements.quote: The honest state of the field.
statements.section: The White Space

statements.quote: The questions can be posed with precision -- ontology, identity, the reality of computation, reference -- because each reduces to a mature debate elsewhere in philosophy.
statements.section: The White Space

statements.quote: The answers cannot yet be given, because each of those debates is itself open.
statements.section: The White Space

statements.quote: And the LLM era has made the questions *new* even where the categories are old: for the first time, the "entity" under discussion is not a hand-written program or a brain but a **learned, high-dimensional object** whose internal structure was not designed but *discovered*, and which we can copy, fork, and merge at will.
statements.section: The White Space

statements.quote: That is exactly the configuration the classical metaphysics of persons and of mathematical objects was not built to handle.
statements.section: The White Space

statements.quote: It is the white space a serious treatment of the metaphysics of AI can claim: not the ethics the field has already filled, but the ontology, identity, and reference of the machine as it actually is.
statements.section: The White Space
